summary:
Rondônia stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted by a 14-1 vote, with joint adoption permitted since 2010 and full marital rights since 2015. The Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018 removed surgery, hormone therapy and diagnosis as conditions for legal gender-marker change, and the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held in ADO 26 and MI 4733 that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitute a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. Federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, so a trans visitor's documents and entry are assessed under the same rules as anyone else's.

Documents remain the sharpest friction. There is no third-gender option in national identity documents, although civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows rectification of gender to a neutral marker and treats the decision as precedent. Gender-marker change otherwise proceeds by self-determination.

Risk of violence does not track the statute. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, most acutely affecting trans people, and enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. The advances themselves face repeal pressure from a conservative Congress.

Political visibility is measurable. Salabert and Hilton became the country's first transgender federal legislators in 2022, and more than 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates stood in the 2024 municipal elections.
tangentialFactors:
Brazil's protections are among the most extensive in Latin America: same-sex marriage, joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised on the same footing as racism.

The legal infrastructure is concentrated in the largest cities. São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming and have established legal support services, while smaller cities and rural areas may present greater social friction despite identical formal rights.

Uneven enforcement is the recurring finding across sources: the statutory protections are broad, but the practical gap between text and experience is where risk concentrates for a trans traveller.
localsOnly:
Residents may change their name and gender marker by self-determination, without surgery, hormones or a diagnosis. Trans voters can register to vote under their lived name and identity even before identity documents have been updated.

Since 2020 it has been possible to record a non-binary or unspecified gender entry at the civil registry, and the Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification to a neutral gender marker while treating the outcome as precedent for later cases.

Discriminatory acts and violence motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity are prosecuted as racism under Law 7.716/1989, with imprisonment of one to five years and fines. National norms on placement of LGBTI people deprived of liberty, and the wider protections discussed in Brazil's national profile, apply in Rondônia as elsewhere in the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses Rondônia state law, state-level police practice, or municipal rules within Rondônia, so conditions specific to Porto Velho and other municipalities in the state are unresolved rather than established.

The inventory contains no reporting on the availability of trans-specific healthcare, shelters or nightlife-safety conditions in Rondônia, and nothing on how the national anti-racisdiction framing of transphobia has been applied by prosecutors in this state.

Whether the 2025 neutral-gender registry precedent has been applied at civil registries in Rondônia is not sourced. Repeal pressure in Congress is reported as a general dynamic with no stated timeline or probability.
